claims.text: Optimizing the synthesis temperature profile synchronizes reduction events among noble-metal precursors.
Synchronizing precursor reduction promotes uniform atomic mixing.
Uniform atomic mixing overcomes kinetic barriers that otherwise cause phase separation during high-entropy alloy nanoparticle formation.
Adjusting the heating ramp rate can promote synchronized reduction.
Near-simultaneous reduction leads to co-nucleation of all precursor species.
Near-simultaneous reduction and co-nucleation facilitate uniform atomic diffusion and mixing.
Enhanced mixing entropy overcomes inherent kinetic differences among the precursors.
Differences in precursor reduction kinetics cause phase separation or elemental segregation when reduction is not synchronized.
An optimized temperature profile will produce homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with uniformly distributed metal atoms.
Standard or unoptimized temperature profiles will produce distinct phases or segregated compositions.
Nanoparticles produced using standard thermal profiles without deliberate synchronization typically exhibit phase separation or inhomogeneous elemental distributions.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal systems containing at least five elements and synthesized through controlled thermal processing.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to binary or ternary systems.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when precursor chemistries have inherently incompatible reduction kinetics.
